mcqs.question: Two candidates face the same "pricing varies by vehicle type" requirement. One says "I'll use Strategy" before writing any code; the other writes a simple if/else first, notices it will grow, then extracts a strategy interface. Which approach do interviewers prefer and why?
options: The second approach, because the pattern was introduced in response to an actual symptom observed in the design, not applied on sight of a familiar-sounding prompt
The first approach, because naming the pattern immediately shows more upfront knowledge
Neither, because design patterns should never be used in LLD interviews
The first approach, because writing an if/else at all is always considered a mistake
mcqs.explanation: Patterns should emerge from a symptom you've actually encountered in your own design, not be applied preemptively because the prompt reminds you of one. The second candidate's if/else wasn't a mistake — it was the evidence that justified extracting the strategy.

mcqs.question: A calculate_fee function has grown a long if/elif chain checking vehicle.type, and every new vehicle type requires editing it again. Which principle is being violated, and what's the fix?
options: The Liskov Substitution Principle is violated; the fix is to remove all subclasses of Vehicle
The Open/Closed Principle is violated; the fix is to extract a pricing strategy interface so new vehicle types add a class instead of editing the function
The Single Responsibility Principle is violated; the fix is to move the function into the Vehicle class
No principle is violated; if/elif chains are the correct way to model type-based variation
mcqs.explanation: A function that must be edited every time a new case is added is not closed to modification — that's the Open/Closed Principle. Extracting a strategy interface lets new vehicle types be added as new classes. Liskov and Single Responsibility aren't the issue here, and the if/elif chain is exactly the growth pattern the principle warns about.

mcqs.question: A candidate says "I'll use the Observer pattern here" but implements a subject that directly calls one hardcoded listener's method, with no way to add a second observer. What's the problem?
options: There is no problem, since the resulting behavior matches Observer closely enough
The problem is only that the code lacks comments explaining the pattern
Naming the pattern without implementing its actual structure — a list of observers that can register and unregister — signals recognition without understanding, which a follow-up question will expose
The problem is that Observer should never be implemented using method calls
mcqs.explanation: Observer's defining structure is a subject that holds and notifies a collection of observers, not a single hardcoded call. Naming the pattern without that structure invites a follow-up that reveals the gap; the issue isn't missing comments or the use of method calls generally.

mcqs.question: A pricing rule has exactly two fixed cases that will never change, but a candidate introduces a Strategy interface, a factory, and two classes to handle it. What's the best assessment?
options: This is good practice, since more design patterns always signal more design maturity
This is acceptable because Strategy is specifically designed for pricing problems
This is only a problem if the interviewer explicitly asks for a simpler solution
This is over-engineering — the added interface and classes provide no real flexibility for a case that isn't actually going to vary, and add unnecessary indirection
mcqs.explanation: Forcing a pattern onto a fixed, unchanging case adds code and indirection without benefit — over-engineering with patterns is still over-engineering. Pattern count isn't a maturity signal, Strategy isn't earned just by touching pricing, and the burden of proof shouldn't fall on the interviewer to ask for simplicity.
